description: Actionable principles for the physical and financial base layer: exercise dose, sleep, saving and investing. For a knowledge worker who wants energy, focus and the freedom to choose work.

notes.front: Why treat fitness and sleep as inputs to cognition rather than lifestyle extras?
notes.back: They set the daily ceiling on attention, working memory and mood; a deficit in either degrades every knowledge task downstream.
notes.analogy: Like power and cooling for a datacenter: not a feature, the precondition for every workload.
notes.extra: Example: One night at 4–5 h sleep gives reaction-time lapses comparable to ~0.05–0.08% blood alcohol. You would not review a design document drunk.

notes.front: WHO minimum weekly aerobic dose for adults?
notes.back: 150–300 min moderate or 75–150 min vigorous activity per week.
notes.extra: Routine: 3 × 30 min brisk walk/cycle commute + longer weekend walk clears the bar.

notes.front: WHO minimum weekly strength dose for adults?
notes.back: Muscle-strengthening on 2+ days per week, covering all major muscle groups.
notes.extra: Routine: 2 × 40 min full-body sessions (e.g. Tue/Fri).

notes.front: What is Zone 2 cardio, and how do you find it without a heart-rate monitor?
notes.back: Steady effort at ~60–70% of max heart rate. Talk test: you can still speak in full sentences.
notes.extra: Routine: 2–3 sessions/week of 45–60 min: conversational-pace cycling or a long walk.

notes.front: Why does Zone 2 cardio matter for a knowledge worker?
notes.back: It builds the aerobic base (mitochondrial density), linked to lower resting heart rate, better sleep and steadier energy through the workday.
notes.analogy: It's building a bigger engine at idle, not redlining it: you get more output for the same effort all day.

notes.front: What is progressive overload?
notes.back: Gradually increasing demand on muscles (weight, reps or sets) so they keep adapting.

notes.front: What happens to a strength programme if you lift the same weight for the same reps every week, and why?
notes.back: Progress stalls: once muscles adapt, the same load is no longer a stimulus. Adaptation needs demand that rises beyond what you can already do.

notes.front: How does double progression apply progressive overload?
notes.back: Pick a rep range (e.g. 8–12). Add reps each session until all sets hit 12, then add ~2.5 kg and drop back to 8.

notes.front: Minimal full-body strength template: which five movement patterns to cover?
notes.back: Squat, hinge, push, pull, carry; 3 sets × 8–12 reps each.
notes.extra: Example: goblet squat, Romanian deadlift, dumbbell press, row/pull-up, farmer's walk. Alternate two sessions (A/B) twice a week.

notes.front: Why is consistency more important than intensity for the cognitive benefits of exercise?
notes.back: The acute effects (attention, mood, BDNF release) last hours, not weeks, so benefits come from frequent doses, not occasional heroic sessions.
notes.analogy: Like caffeine for focus: one huge dose on Saturday doesn't help Tuesday.
notes.extra: Example: A 20-min walk before deep work, five days a week, beats one exhausting Saturday session for weekday focus.

notes.front: Practical rule for using exercise to prime a demanding cognitive task?
notes.back: Do 20–30 min of moderate movement before the task; executive function is improved for ~1–2 h afterwards.
notes.extra: Routine: Walk or cycle, then start the hardest design/writing block within the hour.

notes.front: Does training offset long uninterrupted sitting? What is the countermeasure?
notes.back: No: prolonged sitting raises metabolic and cardiovascular risk even in people who train. Countermeasure: frequent movement breaks, not more gym time.
notes.extra: Routine: Every 45–60 min, stand and move 2–3 min (water refill, walking calls, sit-stand blocks).

notes.front: You train for an hour at 07:00 but then sit for 9 hours. Which risk is untouched, and what would you change?
notes.back: Sitting-related metabolic and cardiovascular risk. Add a short movement break every 30-60 min instead of lengthening the workout.

notes.front: How much sleep do most adults need?
notes.back: 7–9 hours per night.

notes.front: What is the hidden danger of chronic 6-hour nights?
notes.back: Impairment accumulates (after ~10–14 days ≈ one all-nighter) while subjective sleepiness plateaus, so you stop noticing you're impaired.
notes.analogy: Like a slow leak in a tyre: the gauge you check (feeling tired) stops moving while the pressure keeps dropping.

notes.front: What is sleep hygiene?
notes.back: The daily behaviours and bedroom conditions that make it easy to fall asleep, stay asleep and wake at a consistent time.
notes.extra: Examples: fixed wake time, morning light, caffeine cut-off, dim evenings, cool dark bedroom.

notes.front: Which single sleep-hygiene lever has the largest effect, and why?
notes.back: A fixed wake-up time, seven days a week: it anchors the circadian rhythm; bedtime then follows from sleep pressure.
notes.analogy: The wake time is the anchor; bedtime is the boat that drifts into place around it.
notes.extra: Routine: Same alarm Mon–Sun; sleep in at most 45–60 min on weekends to avoid 'social jet lag'.

notes.front: Why does a fixed wake-up time fix a late-night problem better than forcing an earlier bedtime?
notes.back: Waking time anchors the circadian rhythm and builds sleep pressure through the day, so sleepiness arrives at the right hour on its own. Going to bed early without that pressure just means lying awake.

notes.front: Why does morning light matter for sleep?
notes.back: Bright light within ~1 h of waking sets the circadian clock, which schedules melatonin release ~14–16 h later.

notes.front: How much morning light is enough, and why doesn't indoor light count?
notes.back: ~10 min outside on a clear morning, 20–30 min if overcast. Indoor light (~300 lux) is far weaker than outdoors (10,000+ lux even overcast).
notes.extra: Routine: Combine with the walk to work or coffee on the balcony.

notes.front: What is the half-life of caffeine, and what cut-off follows from it?
notes.back: About 5–6 h (3–10 h by genetics). So stop caffeine 8–10 h before bed (e.g. none after 13:00–14:00 for a 23:00 bedtime).
notes.extra: Example: 200 mg at 15:00 → ~100 mg at 21:00 → ~50 mg at 03:00, reducing deep sleep even if you fall asleep fine.

notes.front: You drink a coffee at 17:00 and sleep at 23:00. How much caffeine is still active, and what does this cost you?
notes.back: About half remains (6 h is roughly one half-life). It reduces deep sleep and delays sleep onset even if you do fall asleep.

notes.front: How does even moderate alcohol affect sleep?
notes.back: Faster sleep onset, but it fragments the second half of the night, suppresses REM and raises heart rate.
notes.analogy: Sedation is not sleep: alcohol knocks you out like anaesthesia, then the bill arrives at 3 a.m.
notes.extra: Example: Two glasses of wine at 21:00: asleep at 23:00, awake at 03:00 with a racing pulse.

notes.front: What bedroom conditions support deep sleep?
notes.back: Cool (~18–19 °C), dark, quiet, no screens in bed.
notes.extra: Routine: Thermostat down at 22:00, blackout curtains or eye mask, earplugs, phone charges in the kitchen.

notes.front: What is a wind-down routine, and why does it work?
notes.back: A fixed 30–60 min sequence of low-arousal activities before bed. It works by conditioning: the sequence itself becomes the cue for sleep.
notes.analogy: Like Pavlov's bell: run the same sequence nightly and the body starts preparing for sleep at step one.
notes.extra: Example: dim lights → write tomorrow's top-3 → shower → paper book → lights out.

notes.front: Cut-offs before bed for heavy meals and vigorous exercise?
notes.back: Both about 2–3 h before bed (they raise core temperature/arousal). Light stretching or walking is fine any time.
notes.extra: Example: Dinner by 20:00 and gym at 18:00 rather than 21:30 for a 23:00 bedtime.

notes.front: What should you do if you've been awake in bed for more than ~20 minutes, and why?
notes.back: Get up, go to a dim room, do something boring, return when sleepy. Lying awake trains the brain to link bed with wakefulness (stimulus control, from CBT-I).
notes.extra: Routine: Keep a dim lamp and a dull book in the living room for exactly this.

notes.front: Can you repay sleep debt on the weekend?
notes.back: Only partly: catch-up sleep doesn't fully restore performance and shifts your circadian rhythm, making Monday harder.
notes.extra: Example: Five 6-h nights ≈ 7 h debt. Sleeping until 11:00 Sunday recovers some, then you can't fall asleep before 01:00.

notes.front: What makes a nap restorative rather than groggy?
notes.back: Keep it 10–20 min and before ~15:00, so you wake before deep sleep and don't steal night-time sleep pressure.

notes.front: Why does a coffee nap work?
notes.back: Caffeine takes ~20 min to act: drink coffee, nap 20 min, and wake just as it kicks in.
notes.extra: Routine: 13:30 coffee → 13:35 lie down with a 20-min timer → up at 13:55.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: In what sense does financial literacy buy the freedom to choose work?
notes.back: Savings become runway; enough runway lets you decline bad work, negotiate from strength, retrain or take a risk instead of deciding under duress.
notes.analogy: Runway is the length of the airstrip: the longer it is, the more calmly you can choose when and where to take off.
notes.extra: Example: With 12 months saved, a sabbatical or a lower-paid but better role is a real option; with 1 month, it isn't.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: What is the single most important number in personal finance, and why?
notes.back: The savings rate = (income − spending) / income. It drives runway growth and time to financial independence; returns matter less until the portfolio is large.
notes.extra: Example: ~10% savings rate → ~50 years to independence; 50% → ~17 years (at ~5% real return).

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: How do you compute your runway in months?
notes.back: Liquid savings ÷ average monthly essential spending.
notes.extra: Example: €24,000 ÷ €2,400/month → 10 months.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: What is an emergency fund, and where should it live?
notes.back: 3–6 months of essential expenses (more if income is variable) in an instant-access savings account, separate from current account and investments.
notes.analogy: It's insurance, not an investment: like a spare tyre, its job is to be there, not to earn.
notes.extra: Routine: Automatic payday transfer until the target is reached; never touch it for non-emergencies.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: Your essential spending is 2,000 per month and you have 9,000 saved. What is your runway, and does it fully cover an emergency fund?
notes.back: 9,000 ÷ 2,000 = 4.5 months. It meets the 3–6 month emergency range at the lower half; variable income would need more.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: Emergency fund vs. F-you fund: what is the difference?
notes.back: Emergency fund: covers involuntary shocks (job loss, repairs). F-you fund: a deliberate 6–24-month runway to walk away from a bad situation or take a risk.
notes.extra: Example: Six months saved → you can refuse a disliked role change and take two months to find a better fit.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: What is lifestyle inflation, and what is the countermeasure?
notes.back: Spending rising in step with income, so the savings rate never improves. Counter: pre-commit ≥50% of every raise to automatic saving before it reaches the current account.
notes.analogy: A treadmill that speeds up with every raise: you run faster and stay in the same place.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: Why does a raise do nothing for your freedom if your savings rate stays flat?
notes.back: Runway is built from the gap between income and spending. If spending rises in step, the gap and time to financial independence are unchanged.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: What does pay yourself first mean in practice?
notes.back: Savings and investments move automatically on payday, before discretionary spending; you spend what's left rather than saving what's left.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: What is the 50/30/20 budget split?
notes.back: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings/debt repayment. Treat the 20% as a floor and push it up over time.
notes.extra: Example: €4,000 net → €2,000 needs, €1,200 wants, €800 saved. Aiming for freedom sooner: 50/20/30.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: How should debt be prioritised against investing?
notes.back: Pay off debt with interest above your expected return (~5–7%) first; low-rate mortgage/student debt can sit alongside investing.
notes.analogy: Paying off 18% debt is a guaranteed 18% return; no index fund promises that.
notes.extra: Example: 18% credit card: clear it before buying any ETF. 2% student loan: invest, pay the minimum.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::03 Saving & Runway
notes.front: What is insurance's role in a freedom-oriented plan, and what should you insure?
notes.back: It caps catastrophic downside. Insure large, unlikely losses (liability, disability, health); self-insure small ones.
notes.extra: Example: Disability insurance protects the income that funds everything; an extended laptop warranty doesn't.

notes.front: What is the 4% rule, and what target does it give you?
notes.back: A portfolio of ~25× annual expenses has historically sustained 4% inflation-adjusted withdrawals for 30 years → your FI number.
notes.extra: Example: €30,000/year × 25 = €750,000. For longer horizons many use 3–3.5% (28–33×).

notes.front: What is Coast FI, and why is it relevant to choosing work?
notes.back: The point where untouched investments will grow to your FI number by retirement. After it, work only has to cover current expenses, widening acceptable jobs.
notes.analogy: Like a ball kicked hard enough to roll to the goal on its own: you can stop kicking.
notes.extra: Example: At 35, ~€200,000 at 5% real ≈ €900,000 at 65 with no further contributions.

notes.front: Why does compound growth favour starting early over contributing more later?
notes.back: Growth compounds on prior growth, so early money gets more doubling periods.
notes.analogy: A snowball rolled from the top of the hill ends far bigger than one started halfway down.
notes.extra: Example: At 7%: €10,000 at 25 → ~€160,000 at 65 (4 doublings); the same at 45 → ~€40,000.

notes.front: What is the Rule of 72?
notes.back: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return % (e.g. 7% → ~10 years).

notes.front: Why do fees matter more than they look?
notes.back: They compound negatively: a 1% annual fee over 30 years takes roughly 25% of the final portfolio versus a 0.2% fund. Check the TER.
notes.extra: Example: €500/month for 30 years at 7% gross: ~€566k at 0.2% vs ~€474k at 1%.

notes.front: Two funds earn the same 7% before costs; one charges 1.0% and one 0.2%. Why does the gap widen over time?
notes.back: Fees are deducted every year from a balance that would otherwise compound, so the lost growth itself stops compounding. The difference grows faster than linearly.

notes.front: Why fill tax-advantaged accounts before taxable ones?
notes.back: Tax drag compounds like fees; wrappers that cut taxable income or grow tax-free can raise the effective return by 1–2 points a year.
notes.extra: Routine: Yearly, check contribution room in your pension/retirement wrappers and max them before a taxable brokerage account.

notes.front: What is the case for broad index funds as the core investment?
notes.back: Low cost and diversified across thousands of companies, and most active managers underperform them after fees over 10+ years.
notes.analogy: Buying the haystack instead of searching for the needle.
notes.extra: Routine: Core: a global all-world ETF on automatic monthly purchase. Satellite stock picks capped at ~10–20%.

notes.front: What is asset allocation, and what is the time-horizon rule?
notes.back: The split between equities (long-run growth) and bonds/cash (stability). Money needed within ~5 years shouldn't be in equities.
notes.extra: Example: House deposit in 3 years: cash/short bonds. Retirement 20+ years out: mostly equities.

notes.front: What is sequence-of-returns risk, and how do you mitigate it?
notes.back: When withdrawing, a crash early permanently damages the portfolio; the same crash late barely matters. Mitigate with 1–3 years of expenses in cash/bonds.
notes.analogy: Selling assets in a crash is like selling seed corn in a drought: there's less left to regrow.
notes.extra: Example: Two retirees averaging 6%/yr: −30% in year 1 can run out of money; −30% in year 20 is fine.

notes.front: Why is a 30% crash at age 40 and at the first year of retirement not equivalent?
notes.back: At 40 you are adding money and buy cheaply. In retirement you sell units to fund spending at low prices, so fewer remain to recover (sequence-of-returns risk).

notes.front: What is euro-/dollar-cost averaging, and what is its main benefit?
notes.back: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price. Main value is behavioural: it removes market-timing decisions.
notes.extra: Routine: Standing order on the 1st into the core ETF; never pause it because of headlines.

notes.front: Why is time in the market more reliable than timing the market?
notes.back: Returns cluster in a few days, often next to the worst days; missing the best 10 days over 20 years roughly halves the outcome.
notes.extra: Example: Selling in March 2020 'until things calm down' missed one of the fastest recoveries on record.

notes.front: What is rebalancing, and how often is enough?
notes.back: Restoring the target allocation after market moves. Annually, or when a band (e.g. ±5 points) is breached.
notes.extra: Routine: Every January; direct new contributions to the underweight asset before selling anything.

notes.front: What is the real return, and why plan with it?
notes.back: Nominal return − inflation. Planning with nominal figures overstates future purchasing power.
notes.extra: Example: 7% − 2.5% ≈ 4.5% real. €750k in 25 years buys what ~€400k buys today.

notes.text: Investing behaviour traps: loss aversion → {{c1::selling after drops}}; recency bias → {{c2::chasing last year's winner}}; overconfidence → {{c3::concentrated bets after a few wins}}.
notes.extra: Countermeasure: a written Investment Policy Statement, read before any unplanned trade.

notes.front: What is an Investment Policy Statement (IPS), and what is its job?
notes.back: A one-page written plan: goals, target allocation, contribution and rebalancing rules, prohibited actions (incl. what you do in a 30% drawdown). It makes decisions in calm moments to enforce in turbulent ones.
notes.analogy: Ulysses tied to the mast: you bind your future panicking self while you're still calm.
notes.extra: Example: '80% global equity ETF, 20% bonds. €800 on the 1st. Rebalance annually. No selling in drawdowns. Stocks ≤15%.'

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::05 Systems & Reviews
notes.front: How should fitness and sleep be scheduled relative to work?
notes.back: Block them in the calendar first as recurring appointments, then fit work around them. What's scheduled 'when there's time' gets zero time.
notes.analogy: Big rocks first: put the rocks in the jar before the sand, or they never fit.
notes.extra: Example: Mon/Wed/Fri 07:00 cardio, Tue/Thu 17:30 strength, daily 22:30 wind-down reminder.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::05 Systems & Reviews
notes.front: Weekly fitness & sleep audit: which four numbers do you count?
notes.back: Strength sessions (≥2), cardio minutes (≥150), nights ≥7 h (6/7), days with morning light (7/7). Then adjust next week's calendar, not your intentions.
notes.extra: Routine: Sunday, 5 minutes, habit tracker; the trend matters more than any single week.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::05 Systems & Reviews
notes.front: What is a net-worth statement for, and how often should you update it?
notes.back: Assets minus liabilities on one page: it shows the trend that daily balances hide. Update monthly; compare with 12 months ago, not last month.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::05 Systems & Reviews
notes.front: Annual money review: what are the core checks?
notes.back: Savings rate · net worth vs last year · allocation (rebalance) · fees (>0.3% TER?) · tax wrappers maxed · insurance still fits · FI number updated for inflation.
notes.extra: Routine: 2 hours in the first week of January, same spreadsheet every year.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::05 Systems & Reviews
notes.front: How do fitness, sleep and money literacy reinforce each other?
notes.back: Sleep and exercise protect the cognition that earns income and makes good money decisions; financial runway removes the chronic stress that wrecks sleep and training.
notes.extra: Example: A 03:00 wake-up worrying about rent is a money problem; the fix is an emergency fund, not a sleep app.

notes.deck: Foundations: Fitness, Sleep & Money::05 Systems & Reviews
notes.front: Describe the loop by which poor sleep can worsen your finances, and which step breaks it.
notes.back: Poor sleep impairs judgement and income-earning performance, money stress follows, and stress further damages sleep. Building runway reduces the stress and breaks the loop.
